pixels/words: A transformer reads a sentence as a row of tokens, and attention lets every token look at every other.
pixels/grid: A picture is a grid instead: thirty two by thirty two pixels, with three color values each.
pixels/pixel: The plainest way in is one token per pixel: thirty two times thirty two, one thousand and twenty four tokens.
pixels/cost: But attention scores every token against every other, a T by T grid: over a million scores, in every block, for one tiny picture.
pixels/patch: So cut the picture into small squares, called patches, one token each. In patches of eight by eight pixels, that is just sixteen tokens.
pixels/vit: That is the vision transformer, V I T for short: a plain transformer, the kind built for text, given patches instead of words.
pixels/paper: Alexey Dosovitskiy and colleagues introduced it in 2020, and their title says it: An Image is Worth Sixteen by Sixteen Words.
pixels/scale: Given millions of training images, it matched the best networks built from convolutions.
patches/P: Call the side of a patch P, for patch size. Here P is eight.
patches/side: The picture is H pixels high, H for height: thirty two. So H over P patches, four, fit down each side.
patches/N: Four rows of four: N, the number of patches, is sixteen. N is H over P, squared.
patches/p16: Make P sixteen, and only two patches fit along each side: four in all.
patches/quarter: Doubling P leaves a quarter as many patches, since both sides halve. Halving P gives four times as many.
patches/big: The paper used pictures two hundred and twenty four pixels a side, in patches of sixteen: fourteen squared, one hundred and ninety six patches.
patches/rect: For a picture that is not square, write W for its width: H over P patches fit down, and W over P across.
patches/grid: So a hundred and twenty eight by a hundred and ninety two pixels, in patches of sixteen, is eight down and twelve across: ninety six.
flatten/one: Take one patch, the one with the sun: eight by eight pixels, three color values each, one hundred and ninety two numbers.
flatten/flat: Lay them out in one row: P squared times C numbers, with C for the color channels: three here, one in a gray picture. The row's length depends only on the patch.
flatten/embed: Then, as a word gets an embedding, the row goes through a learned linear map: a weight matrix E, for embedding, plus a bias.
flatten/d: Out comes a token of d numbers, the width the transformer works with: sixty four here.
flatten/shared: Every patch goes through this same map.
flatten/count: Each of the sixty four outputs has one weight per number, one hundred and ninety two, plus a bias: one hundred and ninety three.
flatten/total: Sixty four times one hundred and ninety three: twelve thousand, three hundred and fifty two parameters, for any size of picture.
flatten/conv: That map is a convolution: sixty four filters, each P by P and three channels deep, with a stride of P.
flatten/stride: The stride is how far a filter jumps between stops. Here it jumps a whole patch at a time, so each stop covers exactly one patch.
sequence/stack: Flatten all sixteen patches, one row each: sixteen by one hundred and ninety two. Embedded, they are sixteen tokens of sixty four numbers: the picture is now a sequence.
sequence/cls: One more token goes in front: the class token, learned, from no patch, and the same for every picture. That makes seventeen.
sequence/bag: But attention ignores order. Swap a patch of sky with a patch of grass, and it could not tell.
sequence/pos: So, as with words, each place gets a learned position vector added: seventeen rows of sixty four, the class token's place included.
sequence/blocks: From here it is a plain transformer: each block keeps the shape, seventeen tokens in and seventeen out.
sequence/read: After the last block, the class token has gathered from every patch, and a linear classifier scores it: hence its name.
